div.div: High level overview of the task state machine required to ensure that the two diagnostics causing device resets (and the third causing permanent side effects without reset) are run correctly without causing infinite reset loops.

switch.text: High level overview of the task stat...

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 238px; height: 1px; padding-top: 715px; margin-left: 852px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: rgb(0, 0, 0); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; overflow-wrap: normal;

div.div: This symbol represents "deep history," indicating that the state machine, along with its nested machines and substates, retains its memory across resets. This ensures the task acts as a persistent state machine that will continue in the state it was in before the reset, except for POR and BOR resets which will wipe the history.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 288px; height: 1px; padding-top: 185px; margin-left: 1192px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: rgb(0, 0, 0); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; overflow-wrap: normal;

div.div: The state machine contains submachine states for each reset diagnostic. However, the substates is maintained by the task and passed as input parameters to the diagnostic functions to avoid dependencies between the persistent memory storage service provided by the the Memory Manager and the Diagnostic services provided by the CPU Manager and Watchdog Manager.

box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: rgb(0, 0, 0); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; overflow-wrap: normal;

div.div:
This diagnostic does not reset the device, but has a side-effect of enabling the SWDT (which cannot be disabled again). To avoid this side effect, the diagnostic is run here, before running the WDT Expire diagnostic. This ensures that the SWDT is disabled again when the WDT resets the device.
The API has an input parameter for the new SWDT reset value. This allows the task to set a value that ensures no SWDT error before the WDT Expire diagnostic is finished.
Additionally, if the diagnostic is called last in another task, it can be scheduled as long as the SWDT task timeout accounts for the time it takes to let it expire and the new reset value. E.g. if the task execution time is 10 µs, schedule 9 µs and call the diagnostic with a new reset value of 1 µs (see the way the SWDT is used in the scheduler for context).
